event_54d70037980fae4d.title: Manatee Tempest activity group
event_54d70037980fae4d.description:
The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport

event_cd5b04f46a20926c.title: Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)
event_cd5b04f46a20926c.description:
Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

event_0874d586fa054456.title: System recovery setting tampering
event_0874d586fa054456.description:
System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]

event_f4f380f21a699008.title: SID history injection
event_f4f380f21a699008.description: A Security IDentifcation (SID) history injection was detected on this device. SID history is an attribute that supports migration scenarios. Attackers typically use attack tools to change the SID history of an existing domain user to an SID with elevated privileges. With elevated privileges, the affected process might be able to access sensitive files, ensure persistence, and modify system settings.

A process has injected code into another process, indicating suspicious code being run in the target process memory. Injection is often used to hide malicious code execution within a trusted process. 
As a result, the target process may exhibit abnormal behaviors such as opening a listening port or connecting to a command and control server.

event_0c1bdfc5dfa155bf.title: System executable renamed and launched

Attackers might be attempting to use the executable to perform malicious activities, such as running malicious code or connecting to an attacker-controlled network address. By changing the path or file name of a system executable, attackers can avoid certain behavior-based detection technologies that rely on default paths and file names.

event_de68d32371281529.title: Ongoing hands-on-keyboard attack via Impacket toolkit
event_de68d32371281529.description:
Suspicious execution of a command via Impacket was observed on this device. This tool connects to other hosts to explore network shares and execute commands. Attackers might be attempting to move laterally across the network using this tool. This usage of Impacket has often been observed in hands-on-keyboard attacks, where ransomware and other payloads are installed on target devices.

Corresponding TA for this IOA: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/ff7e4fff-dde3-49be-9a06-7f63a490996d/analystreport
